questiontext.text:
UniCV prototype for Python 3 program questions with checks on the code. The student writes a program (and, if asked, some functions); before the tests are run, the code is analysed statically (without running it) to check the requirements of the question: constructs and syntax that must or must not be used (e.g. a for loop is required and while is forbidden), required functions with their parameters, and limits on print(). If a requirement is not met, the tests are not run and the student sees the list of unmet requirements. As on a console, the values read with input() are echoed to the output.

It replaces python3_IaP, restricted_print_IaP and python3_w_function_check, with the same checks in one question type, plus checks inside each function.

How to write a question

  1. Create a CodeRunner question of type unicv_python3_program. In the question text, state the requirements (e.g. the name and parameters of the function, "do not use while") and the exact text of the prompts and of the output.
  2. In Template params, write the requirements in JSON (all optional, see below), e.g. {"functions": {"inverter_sinal": {"num_params": 1, "require": ["for"]}}, "forbid": ["while", "map", "comprehension"], "lang": "pt"}.
  3. Write the test cases as in any Python program question: the input in Standard Input and the expected output in Expected output. Because input() is echoed, the expected output contains the prompts and the values read, e.g. x? 3.
  4. Optionally, write Test code: it is run after the student's program, with access to its functions, so it can test a function directly (e.g. print(inverter_sinal([1, -2]))). If the program reads data, the test code runs after it has read its input.
  5. Write the solution in the Answer field and keep Validate on save ticked: the solution must meet all the requirements and pass all the tests. A mistake in the template parameters (an unknown name or value) gives "Question error: …", so it is found when the question is saved.

What the student gets

  • The usual Ace code editor.
  • After Check, if the requirements are met, the usual table of tests. Otherwise every test shows "*** Requirements not met ***", the list of unmet requirements (e.g. "The function 'inverter_sinal' must use a for loop.", "The program must not use a while loop.") and "The tests were not run.", so no test is passed.
  • If the program gives an error, a short traceback that shows only the lines of the student's code.

Grading

As in the standard Python question types: each test compares the output with the expected output (EqualityGrader), all or nothing by default.

What can be required or forbidden

The lists require, forbid and only_here (for the whole program, or for one function) take these items:

  • Statements: for, while, if, break, continue, return, def, import, try, with, global, class, lambda.
  • Syntax: list_comprehension ([x for x in a]), set_comprehension, dict_comprehension, generator ((x for x in a), e.g. inside list(…) or sum(…)), comprehension (any of these four), f_string, slicing (a[1:3]), ternary (x if c else y).
  • Operators, written as in Python: +, -, *, /, //, %, ** (each one also matches its augmented assignment, e.g. ** matches x **= 2); +=, -=, *=, /=, //=, %=, **= (only the augmented assignment); ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=, in, not in, is, is not, and, or, not. For example "forbid": ["**"] forbids x ** 0.5, and "require": ["//", "%"] requires integer division and remainder. The unary minus (-x) is not the operator -.
  • Names: any other name is a function, method or variable that must (not) be used, e.g. map, sum, sorted, append, split, input, print. A name is found wherever it is used, not only in calls, so f = map and from math import factorial as f also count as using map and factorial; but a variable, function or parameter that the student defines with that name (e.g. max = lista[0]) is the student's own and is not reported. A dotted name such as math.sqrt is found only written in that form.

Template parameters (all optional)

  • require (default []): items that the program must use.
  • forbid (default []): items that the program must not use.
  • functions (default {}): the functions that the student must write, as an object whose keys are the names of the functions, e.g. {"media": {"num_params": 3}}, or simply a list of names, e.g. ["media"]. Each function must be defined at the top level of the program. For each function:
    • num_params: exact number of parameters (*args and **kwargs are not accepted when it is given).
    • return (default true): the function must return a value with return.
    • call (default true): the function must be called by the program, outside itself and after its definition. Set it to false if only the test code calls it.
    • require (default []): items that the function must use, e.g. ["for"].
    • forbid (default ["input"]): items that the function must not use, e.g. ["input", "print"] so that the reading and writing are done in the main program. Write [] to allow everything.
    • only_here (default []): items that may be used only inside this function, e.g. ["math.sqrt"].
  • max_print: the maximum number of times print may appear in the code (it counts the appearances in the code, not the executions; a print in a loop counts once).
  • max_print_args: the maximum number of arguments of each print.
  • print_regex: a regular expression that the text written by each print of the program must match in full (the arguments joined with sep, without end). Checked while the program runs; a print that does not match stops it with an error. The test code is not checked. In JSON, backslashes are doubled: {"print_regex": "\\d+ \\d+"}.
  • echo_input (default true): input() echoes the value read, as on a console. Set it to false to get plain Python behaviour (the prompt is written, the value is not).
  • lang (default "en"): language of the messages, "en" or "pt".

Unknown parameter names, unknown keys of a function and unknown items give "Question error: …". Parameters whose names start with _ are ignored (they can be used as comments).

Limitations

  • The checks only look at the code: they show that something is used or not, not that it is used in a sensible way (e.g. a required for could be a loop that does nothing).
  • A forbidden name can still be reached in indirect ways (e.g. through getattr or __builtins__), which students of an introductory course are unlikely to use.
  • If a required function is defined more than once, the last definition is checked.

Differences from the question types it replaces

  • From python3_IaP: the parameters require and forbid replace requiredconstructs, proscribedconstructs, proscribedfunctions, proscribedmethods and proscribedsyntactic; generator expressions and the other comprehensions can be forbidden; a forbidden function is also found when it is assigned to a variable.
  • From python3_w_function_check: several functions, with their own required and forbidden items; only_in_function is now only_here and looks at the code, not at the text (comments and strings are ignored).
  • From restricted_print_IaP: the print limits work with stdin and with test code, and together with the other checks.
